content: 1. HIV-uninfected infants or those with unknown HIV status can be fed formula milk under specific conditions. These include ensuring safe water and sanitation at the household and community levels, the caregiver's ability to provide sufficient formula milk to support normal growth and development, and the ability to prepare the formula cleanly and frequently to minimize risks of diarrhea and malnutrition. Additionally, exclusive formula feeding should be practiced for the first six months, with family support for this practice, and access to comprehensive child health services must be available. (Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence) 2. Mothers known to be HIV-infected may consider expressing and heat-treating breast milk as an interim feeding strategy in certain circumstances. These include when the infant is born with low birth weight or is ill and unable to breastfeed, when the mother is temporarily unwell or has a breast health problem such as mastitis, to assist mothers in stopping breastfeeding, or when antiretroviral drugs are temporarily unavailable. (Weak recommendation, very low-quality evidence) 3. For infants and young children known to be HIV-infected, exclusive breastfeeding is strongly encouraged for the first six months of life. Breastfeeding should then continue as per general population recommendations, up to two years or beyond. (Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence) 4. National and local health authorities should actively coordinate and implement services in health facilities, workplaces, communities, and homes to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding among women living with HIV. (Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence) 5. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in the context of mixed feeding. While exclusive breastfeeding is recommended, mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding if ART is available. 6. Mothers living with HIV who do not plan to breastfeed for 12 months can be reassured that shorter durations of breastfeeding are better than not initiating breastfeeding at all. 7. For HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, a regimen with two antiretroviral drugs is effective, but a three-drug regimen is preferred. (Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence) 8. For children aged ≤10 years, AZT + 3TC is the preferred backbone regimen for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis. ABC + 3TC or TDF + 3TC (or FTC) can be considered as alternative regimens. LPV/r is recommended as the preferred third drug for children younger than 10 years. Age-appropriate alternatives include ATV/r, RAL, DRV, EFV, and NVP. (Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence; Conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence) 9. A 28-day prescription of antiretroviral drugs should be provided for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis following an initial risk assessment. (Strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence) 10. Enhanced adherence counseling is suggested for all individuals initiating HIV post-exposure prophylaxis. (Conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence) 11. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants, children, and adolescents with HIV, regardless of clinical and immune conditions. Priority should be given to children under five years old, those with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease, and/or those with CD4 ≤350 cells/mm³. In settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should continue into adulthood, irrespective of ART provision. In low-prevalence settings, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued for children aged five years and older who are clinically stable, virally suppressed on ART for at least six months, and with a CD4 count >350 cells/mm³. (Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence; Conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence) 12. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for HIV-exposed infants from 4 to 6 weeks of age and should continue until HIV infection is excluded by an age-appropriate test after breastfeeding cessation. (Strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence) 13. Children living with HIV who do not have poor weight gain, fever, or current cough are unlikely to have active TB. Those with these symptoms or a contact history with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other conditions. If no TB is found, they should be offered isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) regardless of age. (Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence) 14. Children living with HIV aged more than 12 months who are unlikely to have active TB based on symptom screening and have no contact with a TB case should receive six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV prevention and care. (Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence) 15. Children and young people aged 5–17 years should accumulate at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily. Physical activity beyond 60 minutes daily provides additional health benefits. Most daily physical activity should be aerobic, with vigorous-intensity activities, including those strengthening muscle and bone, incorporated at least three times per week. (Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence) 16. WHO recommends reducing free sugar intake throughout the life course. Adults and children should reduce free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% suggested for additional health benefits. (Strong recommendation; Conditional recommendation) 17. Free sugars include monosaccharides and disaccharides added to foods and beverages, as well as sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, fruit juices, and fruit juice concentrates. Higher free sugar intake threatens nutrient quality by providing energy without specific nutrients. Reducing free sugar intake is associated with parallel changes in body weight. Limiting free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake is based on moderate-quality evidence from observational studies of dental caries. Further limiting intake to less than 5% is based on very low-quality evidence from ecological studies showing a dose-response relationship between free sugar intake and dental caries. (Strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence; Conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence) 18. Low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) is recommended for treating dehydration in HIV-infected and -exposed infants and children with diarrhea. Intravenous electrolyte solution is recommended for severe dehydration. (Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence) 19. Elemental zinc supplementation for 10–14 days is recommended for HIV-infected and -exposed children with diarrhea, at 10 mg/day for infants aged 2–6 months and 20 mg/day for those older than six months. (Strong recommendation, high-quality evidence) 20. Children with dysentery should be treated with ciprofloxacin as a first-line treatment. Ceftriaxone should be used as a second-line treatment in severely ill children where local antimicrobial sensitivity is unknown. (Strong recommendation, low-quality evidence) 21. Xpert MTB/RIF should be used as the initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in children suspected of having multidrug-resistant TB or HIV-associated TB, rather than conventional microscopy and culture. (Strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence)
